summary: Jeremiah 25 (38 verses) continues the story of judgment. Starting with 'The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (this was the first year of ', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows judgment lived out in jerusalem falling. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah (this was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon),
and all the mixed people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, all the kings of the Philistines, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod;
He has left his covert, as the lion; for their land has become an astonishment because of the fierceness of the oppression, and because of his fierce anger.

questions.question: What is happening in Jeremiah 25?
questions.answer: In 38 verses, this chapter jeremiah 25 (38 verses) continues the story of judgment. starting with 'the word that came to jeremiah concerning all the people of judah, in the fourth year of jehoiakim the son of josiah, king of judah (this was the first year of ', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears. The setting is jerusalem falling, written to judah before exile. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Jeremiah and why 25 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally jeremiah, addressed to judah before exile around ~600 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophetic laments — its themes of judgment, new covenant build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'prophet' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Messenger speaking for God. In this chapter, it appears in context of judgment. For a first-time reader: think of it as messenger speaking for god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through judgment and new covenant, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 9 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'behold, I will send and take all the families of the north,” says Yahweh, “and I will send to Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land,...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about judgment. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
